Seeking Private Mental Health Training & Clinical Mentorship Memphis, TN
Hello, everyone!

My name is Shadonna Banks, and I am seeking an experienced LPC-MHSP, licensed psychologist or Psychiatric Mental Health Nurse Practitioner (PMHNP) in the Memphis area who offers private, individualized clinical training, mentorship and professional consultation.

I am currently completing my master’s degree in clinical Mental Health Counseling and already have an established clinical supervisor for my school and internship requirements. I am looking for additional professional development beyond my required supervision hours.

I would love to connect with someone who is willing to provide private, one-on-one teaching and hands-on training in areas such as:

Comprehensive mental health assessments and diagnostic interviewing

DSM-5-TR diagnosis and differential diagnosis

Individual psychotherapy, CBT and other evidence-based approaches

Treatment planning, clinical documentation and progress notes

Trauma-informed care, suicide risk assessment and crisis intervention

Co-occurring mental health and substance use disorders

Psychiatric evaluations, psychotropic medications and collaborative care

Case conceptualization, ethical decision-making and clinical consultation

Working with court-involved clients and individuals referred through federal programs

I am particularly interested in someone who enjoys teaching and is willing to offer structured private sessions, case discussions, practical exercises and opportunities to strengthen my clinical skills.

This is paid professional training and mentorship, not a request for internship placement or supervision hours.

I prefer in-person sessions in Memphis but am open to virtual training. I would love to establish an ongoing professional relationship with someone who can help me continue growing as a mental health professional.

If you provide this type of training or know someone who does, please send me a private message with your credentials, availability, areas of expertise and rates.

Thank you for your recommendations and referrals!

Shadonna Banks, 

LADAC I, Clinical Mental Health Counseling Graduate Student

items.text:
I am looking for some feedback 

When I initially agreed to work with the organization, my understanding was that I would be helping them build and develop their mental health program. The original conversations focused on things like program development, organizational readiness, developing policies and workflows, helping with credentialing preparation, documentation processes, staff training, and potentially providing supervision for MSW interns. I understood my role to be more of a consultant helping them establish the infrastructure needed to provide services.

As I’ve gotten further into the process and received more information, I’m realizing that what they need is much more extensive than I initially understood. They are trying to establish outpatient mental health services, including providing services within schools, but they currently do not have the full clinical and operational infrastructure in place for an outpatient mental health clinic.

There are still significant pieces that need to be established, including policies and procedures, clinical workflows, intake and assessment processes, treatment planning and documentation standards, crisis and suicide-risk procedures, EHR processes, billing and credentialing workflows, quality assurance, and clarification of the clinical leadership structure.

One of my biggest concerns is that I’ve now learned they need a licensed clinician’s credentials to be listed as part of their credentialing/application process. That feels very different from simply consulting with an organization on how to build a program. I do not want my license or credentials attached to an organization in a way that could make me responsible for clinical oversight, billing, supervision, or the operation of the program when I am not functioning as their Clinical Director or providing that level of ongoing oversight.

I work a full-time job, and only have limited availability to provide consulting services. Because of that, I’m questioning whether what they actually need is a dedicated Clinical Director or another licensed clinician who is formally responsible for the clinical operations, while I remain in a separate consulting role.

Based on this situation, how would you recommend I proceed? Would you continue strictly as a consultant with very clearly defined boundaries and decline to have your license used for credentialing/clinical oversight, or would you step away altogether until the organization has the appropriate clinical leadership and infrastructure in place? I especially want to make sure I’m protecting my license and not unintentionally accepting legal, ethical, or clinical responsibility that goes beyond the role I originally agreed to. Even though I agreed without really understanding until I received miore information

topComments.text: I agree they need a dedicated clinical director and it may be more of a risk for you

Georgia Therapists  I’d love to connect with you!

 

My name is Tremayne Rippy, and I’m the founder of Male Trauma Matters (MTM), a Georgia nonprofit focused on helping males from boys and teens to fathers, veterans, and adult men connect with resources that can help them address trauma, heal, and move forward.

 

Right now, one of my biggest priorities is building a trusted referral network of therapists and mental health professionals throughout Georgia.

 

I’m looking to connect with licensed therapists, counselors, group practices, clinics, and Georgia licensed telehealth providers who work in areas such as trauma, PTSD, childhood trauma, domestic violence, sexual abuse, grief, veterans, fatherhood/family issues, anger, relationships, and other challenges affecting males.

 

This isn't a request for therapists to provide free services. I want to build relationships with professionals already doing this work so that when a male reaches out to MTM for help, we have trusted resources within our network to connect him with.

 

For therapists interested in doing more, I’m also looking for Program Partners for Change Starts Here, a program under MTM’s Breaking Silence initiative. Program Partners may have opportunities to collaborate with MTM on workshops, educational content, community events, support initiatives, and other efforts focused on helping males access mental health support, address trauma, and begin the healing process.

 

MTM is still growing, and I believe the best way to build this correctly is with professionals at the table from the beginning. I’d also love to hear what you’re seeing in your work—where are males falling through the cracks, what barriers are keeping them from seeking or continuing therapy, and what resources are missing?

About the Partner Application

The Community Partner Application takes approximately 10–15 minutes to complete. I know it's a little more detailed than a typical interest form, and that's intentional.

 

For many men, trust is already a major barrier to seeking help. Some may be reaching out for the first time, while others may have tried counseling or other services before and walked away feeling unheard, misunderstood, or that they didn't receive the support they were looking for.

 

That's why MTM wants to take the time to learn about the professionals in our network the populations you serve, your areas of expertise, credentials, services, approach, and how you may want to contribute to the mission.

 

We're not trying to build the biggest referral list. We're trying to build a trusted one.

 

Completing the application does not create a commitment or guarantee partnership approval. It gives us the information needed to determine whether there may be a good fit and helps us prepare for the Partner Introduction & Review Meeting.

 

If this mission aligns with you or your practice, I’d love to connect. You can complete the application below, or feel free to message me directly if you'd rather have a conversation first.

 

Ready to learn more? The application explains everything you need to know about partnering with MTM.

 

⏱️ Estimated time: 10–15 minutes

🔗 Community Partner Application:

https://forms.gle/pYHLQoocfCQXBC4x8

 

Male Trauma Matters
*Breaking Silence. Building Purpose.*

 

Every partner brings something different to the table. MTM brings those strengths together to build stronger pathways to support, healing, and opportunity.

As fall sets in and the final quarter of the year arrives, staying on top of your Accounts Receivable (A/R) is the single best way to protect your revenue. Waiting until December to review aging claims often means leaving money on the table.

Here are 5 key reasons why consistent A/R tracking is essential right now:

Beat Strict Timely Filing Limits: Insurance payers enforce tight deadlines for initial claims, corrections, and appeals. Catching 60+, 90+, and 120+ day balances now ensures you have enough time to appeal and collect before claims expire permanently.

Prepare for Patient Deductible Resets: Patients scramble to schedule appointments before their coverage resets on January 1st. Clear A/R tracking keeps your patient statements up to date so co-pays and deductibles don't fall behind.

Uncover and Fix Payer Denial Trends: Detailed tracking highlights patterns—like recurring missing documentation or specific clearinghouse delays—allowing you to fix root causes rather than endlessly chasing individual denials.

Stabilize Year-End Cash Flow: Uncollected claims stall your practice's income stream. Cleaning up aging accounts late in the year gives you the predictable cash flow needed for annual bonuses, tax prep, and operating expenses.

Start the New Year with a Clean Slate: Wiping out outdated balances now means you won't enter January bogged down by old debt, letting your staff focus on growth and patient care in the new year.

Don't let your hard-earned revenue drift into next year. Let’s clean up your accounts receivable and make sure every claim gets paid! 📊💰

📩 Want a clearer picture of your practice's financial health? Send a message to set up an A/R review today!

Quick question if you're planning to open a private practice this year. Do you know when your credentialing applications actually need to go in?

Credentialing can take 90 to 180 days with a single insurance payer, and that clock usually starts moving long before you see your first client, not after.

So if you've already got an opening date in your head, it's worth checking that date against this timeline. A lot of new practice owners plan everything else first and treat credentialing like something they'll deal with once the doors are open.

We laid out the full pre-opening order in a free workbook, credentialing included. Comment "workbook" and we'll send it your way.

Got a friend who's planning to open a practice? They'll thank you for this now more than after they've already picked a date.
